rationale.goldenRule: Beck's Triad = Hypotension, Muffled Sounds, JVD (Tamponade).

content.chiefComplaint: Sudden decrease in chest tube output and hypotension.

nursesNotes.author: RN CVICU
nursesNotes.entry: Patient is POD #1 s/p CABG x 4. Extubated at 1000. Mediastinal chest tubes draining serosanguinous fluid approx 50-60 mL/hr. Patient alert, cooperative, using incentive spirometer.

nursesNotes.author: RN CVICU
nursesNotes.entry: Sudden change in status. Chest tube output dropped to 0 mL in last hour. Patient appears restless and anxious. Heart sounds appear muffled compared to prior exam. Neck veins distended. Monitor shows Sinus Tachycardia. BP dropped from 110/70 to 88/62. Surgeon notified STAT.

historyPhysical.hpi: 58-year-old male, POD 1 after Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG). Recovery was uneventful until 1500 when nurse noted cessation of chest tube drainage. Patient became agitated, complaining of 'pressure' in chest (distinct from incisional pain).

physicalExam.cardiovascular: Distant heart sounds, JVD present at 45 degrees, Pulsus Paradoxus noted on art line

radiology.findings: Large pericardial effusion with right ventricular diastolic collapse. Swinging heart motion noted.

rationale.coreConcept: Cardiac Tamponade is a mechanical obstruction of cardiac filling caused by fluid accumulation in the pericardial sac.
rationale.caseSummary: A post-CABG patient develops sudden cessation of chest tube drainage (suggesting a clot/blockage), followed by signs of obstructive shock (hypotension, JVD, muffled heart sounds). This is a surgical emergency.
rationale.answerAnalysis: The key is recognizing Beck's Triad (Hypotension, JVD, Muffled Heart Sounds) combined with the 'clotted tube' history. The heart cannot fill because it is being squeezed by trapped blood.
rationale.trap: Assuming the drop in chest tube output is a 'good sign' that bleeding has stopped. In the context of hypotension, sudden cessation means blockage and retention of blood (Tamponade).
rationale.goldenRule: Sudden stop in chest tube drainage + Hypotension = Tamponade until proven otherwise.

steps.description: Identify Beck's Triad and cessation of drainage.
Fluid is trapping the heart, preventing diastolic filling.

difficulty.label: Evaluation
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Differentiate Obstructive Shock from Hypovolemic Shock. Hypovolemic = Flat neck veins. Obstructive (Tamponade) = Distended neck veins.

mnemonic.title: Beck's Triad
mnemonic.content: 3 D's: Distant heart sounds, Distended neck veins, Decreased arterial pressure.

cheatSheet.title: Tamponade Clues
points: Equalization of cardiac pressures (CVP = PAD = PCWP).

referenceInfo.anatomy: Pericardium is a fibrous sac. It does not stretch acutely. Even 100-200mL of rapid blood accumulation can crush the ventricles.
referenceInfo.physiology: Obstructive Shock: Compression -> Decreased Diastolic Filling -> Decreased Stroke Volume -> Decreased Cardiac Output -> Hypotension.
referenceInfo.pharm: Fluids/Pressors are a temporary bridge. The definitive treatment is mechanical drainage.

history.note: Patient is POD #1 s/p CABG x 4. Extubated at 1000. Mediastinal chest tubes draining serosanguinous fluid approx 50-60 mL/hr. Patient alert, cooperative, using incentive spirometer.

Sudden change in status. Chest tube output dropped to 0 mL in last hour. Patient appears restless and anxious. Heart sounds appear muffled compared to prior exam. Neck veins distended. Monitor shows Sinus Tachycardia. BP dropped from 110/70 to 88/62. Surgeon notified STAT.

historyPhysical.hpi: 58-year-old male, POD 1 after Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG). Recovery was uneventful until 1500 when nurse noted cessation of chest tube drainage. Patient became agitated, complaining of 'pressure' in chest (distinct from incisional pain).

physicalExam.cardiovascular: Distant heart sounds, JVD present at 45 degrees, Pulsus Paradoxus noted on art line

radiology.findings: Large pericardial effusion with right ventricular diastolic collapse. Swinging heart motion noted.

rationale.coreConcept: Recognizing the clinical signature of Tamponade.
rationale.caseSummary: Patient exhibits classic obstructive shock signs.
rationale.answerAnalysis: The combination of Hypotension (h7), JVD (h4), and Muffled Sounds (h3) is Beck's Triad. 0 mL output (h1) suggests the cause (trapped blood). Pulsus Paradoxus (h6) is the hallmark hemodynamic finding.
rationale.trap: Selecting 'Restless' (h2). While true, it is non-specific (could be pain, hypoxia, etc.). Tamponade has specific mechanical signs.
rationale.goldenRule: Clear lungs + JVD + Hypotension = Obstructive Shock (Tamponade or PE).

rationales.h1,: [Hook] Chest tube 0 mL. [Breakdown] Highly suspicious in a post-op patient who was draining 50mL/hr. Suggests obstruction/clot, leading to retention. [Trap] Thinking bleeding stopped naturally.
rationales.h3,: [Hook] Distant heart sounds. [Breakdown] Fluid insulates the sound of valves closing. Part of Beck's Triad. [Trap] Attributing to obesity/vent noise.
rationales.h4,: [Hook] JVD. [Breakdown] Blood cannot enter the heart, backing up into jugulars. Part of Beck's Triad. [Trap] Thinking it's fluid overload.
rationales.h6,: [Hook] Pulsus Paradoxus. [Breakdown] Exaggerated drop in BP during inspiration due to ventricular interdependence. Specific to Tamponade. [Trap] Ignoring waveform changes.
rationales.h7,: [Hook] BP 88/62. [Breakdown] Obstructive shock. Part of Beck's Triad. [Trap] Thinking it's just hypovolemia.
rationales.h2,: [Hook] Restless. [Breakdown] Sign of hypoxia/hypoperfusion but non-specific. [Trap] Focusing on behavior vs. physiology.
rationales.h5,: [Hook] Lungs clear. [Breakdown] Confirms this is NOT heart failure (Cardiogenic Shock). Important negative finding. [Trap] Irrelevant as a positive sign of tamponade.

screens.prompt: Distinguish between Hypovolemic Shock, Cardiogenic Shock, and Obstructive Shock (Tamponade) based on findings.

rows.rationale: In hypovolemia, neck veins are flat. In Tamponade, they are distended.
Specific to fluid surrounding the heart.
Cardiogenic shock causes backup into lungs. Tamponade lungs are typically clear.

rows.text: Sudden cessation of chest tube output
rows.rationale: Suggests the mechanism of fluid trapping.
Hallmark of low volume.

rationale.coreConcept: Differential diagnosis of shock states in CVICU.
rationale.caseSummary: Patient has JVD + Clear Lungs + Hypotension. This rules out Hypovolemia (would have flat veins) and Cardiogenic (would have wet lungs).
rationale.answerAnalysis: Tamponade is unique: The heart is 'choked' so systemic veins are full (JVD), but the lungs are dry because the right heart can't pump blood into them.
rationale.trap: Confusing JVD in Heart Failure vs Tamponade. Both have JVD, but Heart Failure has Wet Lungs. Tamponade has Dry Lungs.
rationale.goldenRule: JVD + Dry Lungs = Obstruction (Tamponade/PE). JVD + Wet Lungs = Failure.

mnemonic.content: Hypovolemic = Empty Tank. Cardiogenic = Broken Pump. Obstructive = Blocked Pump.

rationale.caseSummary: Patient needs decompression.
rationale.answerAnalysis: 1. Notify: Need a doctor to drain it. 2. Fluids: Fill the tank to keep the heart open against pressure (temporizing). 3. Echo: Confirm. 4. Meds: Last.
rationale.trap: Withholding fluids because of JVD. In Tamponade, you MUST give fluids to increase intracardiac pressure to overcome the pericardial pressure, even if JVD is present.
rationale.goldenRule: In Tamponade, FLUIDS are the bridge to SURGERY.

mnemonic.title: Fill & Drain
mnemonic.content: Fill the tank (Fluids), Drain the sac (Surgery).

cheatSheet.title: Intervention Pearls
points: Keep heart rate high (CO depends on HR since SV is fixed).

referenceInfo.anatomy: Right Ventricle is thin-walled and collapses first.
referenceInfo.physiology: Increasing preload (fluids) increases RV pressure, resisting collapse.
referenceInfo.pharm: Volume expansion is the only medical therapy that helps.

rationale.caseSummary: Post-CABG Tamponade requires reopening the chest.
rationale.answerAnalysis: Condition: Tamponade. Actions: Fluids (temporize) + Surgery (fix). Parameters: BP (perfusion) + Chest Tube (resolution of block). Lasix/Nitro decrease preload and are FATAL in tamponade.
rationale.trap: Administering Lasix (a3) because of JVD. This is the 'death trap'. The heart is starved of volume; removing more volume causes immediate arrest.
rationale.goldenRule: Never diurese a Tamponade patient, even if they look fluid overloaded.

mnemonic.title: Avoid D-N-M
mnemonic.content: No Diuretics, No Nitrates, No Morphine (vasodilators).

cheatSheet.title: Tamponade Code
points: PEA is the most common arrest rhythm in Tamponade.
If patient arrests -> Emergency Thoracotomy at bedside.
CPR is ineffective because the heart is empty.

referenceInfo.physiology: Releasing the blood restores diastolic filling immediately.
referenceInfo.pharm: Epinephrine may be used to maintain HR/Contractility.

Distributive is sepsis/anaphylaxis (vasodilation), not obstruction.
Vasodilators reduce venous return.
Fluids are indicated, not avoided.
The heart is preload-dependent to overcome the squeeze.
Reducing afterload helps; reducing preload kills.

rationale.caseSummary: Understanding WHY drugs are safe or dangerous.
rationale.answerAnalysis: Tamponade = Obstructive. Nitro = Vasodilation = Low Preload. Low Preload = Empty Heart = Arrest.
rationale.trap: Thinking Nitro is always good for 'heart patients'. In this specific mechanical problem, it is lethal.
rationale.goldenRule: Preload is King in Tamponade.

mnemonic.title: Squeeze Needs Flow
mnemonic.content: If the heart is squeezed, it needs flow (volume) to stay open.

referenceInfo.physiology: Frank-Starling law: normally more stretch = more squeeze. Here, external pressure prevents stretch.

options.rationale: Indicates restoration of cardiac output.
Indicates the blockage is cleared.
Fluid insulation is removed.
JVD should resolve as RA pressure drops.
Pulsus paradoxus should disappear with resolution.

rationale.caseSummary: Post-procedure assessment.
rationale.answerAnalysis: BP normalizes, Drain works, Sounds clear. Persistence of JVD or Pulsus Paradoxus means the tamponade is NOT fixed.
rationale.trap: Checking the 'Chest Tube Output' as a negative. In this case, RESUMING output is good (it means the clot is gone and the blood is leaving the chest).
rationale.goldenRule: Immediate hemodynamic improvement is expected upon drainage.

mnemonic.title: Resolution Triad
mnemonic.content: BP up, JVD down, Sounds loud.

points: Watch for 'drainage dump' (large volume out initially).

referenceInfo.physiology: Return of normal diastolic filling.

nursesNotes.entry: Patient presents with crushing substernal chest pain onset 90 minutes ago while shoveling snow. Pain 8/10, radiating to left arm and jaw. Associated with nausea, diaphoresis, and sense of impending doom. Skin is pale, cool, diaphoretic. Patient vomited once en route.

nursesNotes.author: ED Primary RN
nursesNotes.entry: 12-lead ECG completed showing 5-6 mm ST elevation in leads V1-V4 with reciprocal ST depression in inferior leads. Patient noted to have bradycardia with heart rate 48 bpm and hypotension 88/54 mmHg. Cath Lab activated. Placed on cardiac monitor - 3rd degree AV block identified with ventricular escape rhythm. Transcutaneous pacing pads applied.

ecg.findings: ST elevation 5-6mm in V1-V4 (Anterior wall). Reciprocal ST depression II, III, aVF. 3rd Degree AV Block with ventricular escape rhythm at 48 bpm.
ecg.interpretation: Acute Anterior STEMI with Complete Heart Block

rationale.coreConcept: Management of Anterior STEMI complicated by Complete Heart Block and Cardiogenic Shock
rationale.caseSummary: Patient with Anterior STEMI (LAD occlusion) presents with 3rd degree AV block and hemodynamic compromise (Bradycardia + Hypotension). This is a life-threatening electrical and mechanical crisis requiring immediate reperfusion and pacing support.
rationale.answerAnalysis: Anterior MI affects the LAD territory, which supplies the septum containing the AV node conduction system and the majority of LV muscle mass. Complete heart block eliminates atrial contribution to cardiac output, and the slow ventricular escape rhythm combined with massive MI causes shock. Atropine may help temporarily, but transcutaneous or transvenous pacing is often required. Morphine and Nitroglycerin are contraindicated due to hypotension and possible RV involvement.
rationale.trap: Administering Nitroglycerin or Morphine to a hypotensive STEMI patient. Both cause vasodilation and can precipitate cardiovascular collapse, especially with RV infarct or bradycardia.
rationale.goldenRule: Never give Nitrates or Morphine if SBP < 90 mmHg or HR < 50 bpm in acute MI.

steps.description: Identify STEMI + Complete AV Block + Hypotension as a triad of danger.
Understand that LAD occlusion affects both pump function and electrical conduction.
Prepare for emergency PCI, treat bradycardia with Atropine/Pacing, avoid vasodilators.

difficulty.label: Evaluation
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Recognize the constellation of Anterior STEMI + Complete Heart Block as a medical emergency requiring pacing and immediate revascularization. Avoid reflexive use of standard MI meds without assessing BP and HR.

mnemonic.title: MONA-GREETS
mnemonic.content: Morphine, Oxygen, Nitrates, Aspirin - but use caution with M and N if BP low or HR low (GREETS = Get Ready for Exceptions, Evaluate, Treat Shock)
mnemonic.explanation: Traditional MONA is outdated. Must assess hemodynamics first.

cheatSheet.title: STEMI Contraindications
points: NO Nitrates if SBP < 90 or RV infarct (look at inferior leads)
NO Beta-Blockers if bradycardic or in shock

referenceInfo.anatomy: The Left Anterior Descending (LAD) artery supplies the anterior wall, apex, and interventricular septum of the heart. The septum contains the Bundle of His and bundle branches. Proximal LAD occlusion can damage the conduction system, causing AV blocks.
referenceInfo.physiology: Complete (3rd degree) AV block occurs when atrial impulses cannot reach the ventricles. The ventricles generate their own escape rhythm (usually 20-40 bpm), which is inadequate for cardiac output. Hypotension results from both the slow rate and the loss of atrial kick (which normally contributes 20-30% of ventricular filling).
referenceInfo.pharm: Atropine blocks vagal (parasympathetic) tone and can increase heart rate if the block is at the AV node level. However, in infranodal blocks (below the AV node), Atropine is less effective and pacing is required. Morphine causes histamine release leading to vasodilation and bradycardia - dangerous in this scenario.

rationale.coreConcept: Recognition of High-Risk STEMI with Complications
rationale.caseSummary: Patient presents with Anterior STEMI complicated by complete heart block and cardiogenic shock, creating a perfect storm requiring immediate aggressive intervention.
rationale.answerAnalysis: The critical findings are: prolonged chest pain with ST elevation (STEMI diagnosis), severe bradycardia (HR 48), hypotension (shock), and complete heart block (electrical emergency). These create immediate life threat requiring Cath Lab activation and pacing. Risk factors and diaphoresis, while important for context, are not immediate intervention triggers.
rationale.trap: Focusing on risk factors (smoking h1) or general appearance (diaphoresis h6) rather than the life-threatening triad of STEMI + Bradycardia + Hypotension.
rationale.goldenRule: Time = Muscle. STEMI + Heart Block + Hypotension = Immediate PCI + Pacing.

steps.description: Identify the triad: Ischemia (STEMI) + Electrical failure (Heart Block) + Pump failure (Hypotension).
Understand this is not a simple STEMI but a complex case with multiple simultaneous threats.
Activate Cath Lab, prepare pacing, avoid vasodilators.

mnemonic.title: B-B-B
mnemonic.content: Bad BP, Bad Beat, Bad Block = Big trouble.
mnemonic.explanation: Reminds you that hypotension, bradycardia, and heart block together are catastrophic.

cheatSheet.title: STEMI Warning Signs
points: Anterior STEMI: Higher risk of pump failure and conduction blocks
Complete Heart Block: Often requires temporary pacing

referenceInfo.anatomy: The LAD supplies the interventricular septum which contains the Bundle of His and proximal bundle branches.

nursesNotes.entry: Patient is cool, clammy, and confused. Crackles auscultated bilaterally. S3 gallop present. Urine output 10 mL in past hour.

rationale.caseSummary: Patient presents with classic signs of cardiogenic shock post-MI: hypotension, pulmonary congestion (crackles), and hypoperfusion (cool skin, oliguria, high lactate).
rationale.answerAnalysis: In cardiogenic shock, the 'pump' fails. This leads to backup of blood (High PCWP/Preload) and inability to pump forward (Low Cardiac Output). The body compensates by clamping down vessels (High SVR/Afterload) to maintain BP, which unfortunately worsens the strain on the failing heart.
rationale.trap: Thinking SVR is low because BP is low. In Cardiogenic shock, SVR is paradoxically HIGH as a compensatory mechanism (unlike Septic shock where SVR is low).
rationale.goldenRule: Cardiogenic Shock = High Preload + High Afterload + Low Contractility.

steps.description: Identify signs of 'Cold and Wet' shock (hypoperfusion + congestion).
Correlate clinical findings with hemodynamic parameters (High PCWP, Low CI).
Select interventions that improve contractility without increasing afterload (e.g., Dobutamine).

mnemonic.explanation: Describes the hemodynamic profile of cardiogenic shock.

Hypovolemic: Low PCWP, High SVR, Low CO

referenceInfo.anatomy: Left Ventricle failure leads to backup into Pulmonary Capillaries.
referenceInfo.physiology: Pulmonary Capillary Wedge Pressure (PCWP) reflects Left Ventricular End Diastolic Pressure (LVEDP). High LVEDP causes pulmonary edema.
referenceInfo.pharm: Dobutamine is a beta-1 agonist inotrope used to increase cardiac output and mildly decrease SVR.

structure.prompt: Complete the sentence regarding the patient's hemodynamic status.
structure.text: The patient's clinical presentation is consistent with %{d1}, characterized hemodynamically by a %{d2} Pulmonary Capillary Wedge Pressure (PCWP) and a %{d3} Systemic Vascular Resistance (SVR).

d1,.whyCorrect: The combination of hypotension (BP 84/48), pulmonary congestion (crackles), and signs of poor perfusion (cool skin, lactate 4.5) following a recent MI is classic for Cardiogenic Shock.

distractorRationales.o2,: Distributive Shock (like Sepsis) typically presents with warm skin and bounding pulses initially, and would not necessarily cause the pulmonary congestion seen here.

d2,.whyCorrect: In Cardiogenic Shock, the failing left ventricle cannot pump forward effectively, causing blood to back up into the lungs, resulting in a HIGH PCWP (Preload) and pulmonary edema.

distractorRationales.o4,: A Low PCWP indicates hypovolemia (empty tank), which contradicts the finding of crackles/congestion (full tank/wet lungs).

d3,.whyCorrect: In response to low cardiac output and hypotension, the sympathetic nervous system causes intense vasoconstriction to maintain blood pressure, resulting in a HIGH SVR (Afterload). This manifests clinically as cool, clammy skin.

distractorRationales.o6,: Low SVR is characteristic of Distributive Shock (vasodilation), which would present with warm, flushed skin, not the cool/clammy skin seen in this patient.

rationale.caseSummary: Patient has Atrial Fibrillation with Rapid Ventricular Response (RVR) causing hemodynamic instability (Hypotension).
rationale.answerAnalysis: Unstable tachycardia (defined by hypotension, altered mental status, or ischemic chest pain) requires immediate Synchronized Cardioversion. Rate control medications (Diltiazem/Metoprolol) are for STABLE patients. Defibrillation (unsynchronized) is for pulseless arrest (VF/VT).
rationale.trap: Giving Diltiazem because it's a 'rate control' problem. While true, the HYPOTENSION makes it an electrical emergency requiring cardioversion first.
rationale.goldenRule: Unstable Tachycardia = Electricity (Synchronized Cardioversion).

referenceInfo.anatomy: AV Node conducts atrial impulses to ventricles.
referenceInfo.physiology: Rapid rate reduces diastolic filling time, causing drop in stroke volume and hypotension. Restoring sinus rhythm restores 'atrial kick' (20-30% of CO).

structure.text: Due to the patient's %{d1}, the priority intervention is %{d2}. The nurse must ensure the defibrillator is in %{d3} mode to prevent R-on-T phenomenon.

d1,.whyCorrect: The patient is hypotensive (BP 88/60) and symptomatic (dizziness), defining this as 'Unstable Tachycardia'.

d2,.whyCorrect: Synchronized Cardioversion is the ACLS standard for Unstable Tachycardia with a pulse. It times the shock to avoid the vulnerable T-wave.

distractorRationales.o4,: IV Diltiazem is for STABLE tachycardia. Giving a calcium channel blocker to a hypotensive patient can cause cardiovascular collapse.
distractorRationales.o5,: Unsynchronized defibrillation is for PULSELESS arrest (VF/pVT). Shocking unsynchronized on a perfusing rhythm can induce V-Fib.

d3,.whyCorrect: SYNC mode allows the machine to identify the R-wave and deliver energy safely. Failing to sync can cause the shock to land on the T-wave (R-on-T), triggering V-Fib.

distractorRationales.o7,: ASYNC mode is for defibrillation or pacing, not cardioversion of a perfusing rhythm.

rationale.caseSummary: Patient presents with classic signs of Aortic Dissection: Tearing pain, Hypertension, Marfan's history, and pulse deficits/BP discrepancy.
rationale.answerAnalysis: The priority in aortic dissection is 'Anti-Impulse Therapy' to reduce shear stress on the aortic wall. This involves controlling Heart Rate first (Beta Blockers) and THEN Blood Pressure (Nitroprusside/Vasodilators). Lowering BP without lowering HR first causes reflex tachycardia, increasing shear stress and propagation of the tear.
rationale.trap: Giving Vasodilators (Nitroprusside) first to fix the high BP. This causes reflex tachycardia (increased dP/dt), which can rip the aorta further.
rationale.goldenRule: Beta Blockers FIRST, then Vasodilators.

steps.description: Identify Dissection triad (Pain, Pulse deficit, HTN).
Goal is to reduce shear stress (Heart Rate and BP).

difficulty.label: Evaluation
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Strict ordering of medications is critical to prevent rupture.

mnemonic.title: B before V
mnemonic.content: Beta-blocker before Vasodilator.

referenceInfo.anatomy: Intimal tear allows blood to separate aortic wall layers.
referenceInfo.physiology: Shear stress (dP/dt) depends on Heart Rate and contractility. Beta blockers reduce both.
referenceInfo.pharm: Esmolol is an ultra-short acting beta blocker ideal for rapid titration.

structure.prompt: Complete the medication administration strategy.
structure.text: The nurse anticipates an order for %{d1} as the priority intervention to reduce aortic wall shear stress. Once heart rate is controlled, %{d2} may be added if systolic blood pressure remains > 120 mmHg.

d1,.whyCorrect: IV Esmolol is the priority to lower heart rate and contractility (Anti-Impulse Therapy). This reduces the shear force (dP/dt) that propagates the dissection.

distractorRationales.o2,: Nitroprusside given alone causes reflex tachycardia, which increases shear stress and can worsen the dissection/cause rupture.
distractorRationales.o3,: Hydralazine causes significant reflex tachycardia and is contraindicated in acute dissection.

d2,.whyCorrect: After heart rate is controlled (blunting the reflex tachycardia response), a vasodilator like Nitroprusside is added to strictly control SBP to 100-120 mmHg.

distractorRationales.o5,: Inotropes increase contractility and shear stress, directly worsening the dissection risk.

rationale.caseSummary: Sudden cessation of chest tube output + Hypotension + Rising CVP + Tachycardia = Cardiac Tamponade (Beck's Triad elements).
rationale.answerAnalysis: The clot in the chest tube trapped blood in the pericardial space. This external pressure compresses the heart, preventing filling. CVP rises (backup), BP falls (no output), and sounds muffle. Treatment is decompression (milking tubes or thoracotomy), NOT fluids or pressors.
rationale.trap: Increasing pressors/fluids for the hypotension. This is obstructive shock; the pump is being squeezed. You must relieve the squeeze.
rationale.goldenRule: Sudden stop in chest tube drainage + Hypotension = Tamponade.

structure.prompt: Complete the assessment interpretation.
structure.text: The patient is exhibiting signs of %{d1} shock due to %{d2}. The sudden cessation of chest tube output suggests %{d3}.

d1,.whyCorrect: Obstructive shock occurs when physical pressure prevents the heart from filling or pumping, evidenced here by rising CVP (backup) despite falling BP (no output).

distractorRationales.o2,: Hypovolemic shock would typically present with LOW CVP (empty tank), whereas this patient has rising CVP (obstructed tank).

d2,.whyCorrect: Beck's Triad (Hypotension, Muffled Sounds, High CVP/JVD) in a post-op cardiac patient is classic for Cardiac Tamponade.

distractorRationales.o4,: Graft hemorrhage would lead to high chest tube output and signs of hypovolemia, not the rising CVP and muffled sounds seen here.

d3,.whyCorrect: Sudden cessation of drainage often indicates a clot blocking the tube, trapping blood around the heart and causing the tamponade.

distractorRationales.o6,: Bleeding rarely stops 'suddenly' to zero. A gradual taper is normal; sudden stop suggests obstruction.

rationale.caseSummary: Inferior STEMI (II, III, aVF) + V4R elevation + Hypotension + Clear Lungs + JVD = Right Ventricular Infarction.
rationale.answerAnalysis: The Right Ventricle is failing. It is PRELOAD DEPENDENT. It needs volume to push blood through the lungs to the LV. Nitroglycerin reduces preload and is deadly here (drops BP to zero). Treatment is IV Fluid Bolus to maximize preload.
rationale.trap: Giving Nitroglycerin because it's a STEMI. In RV infarcts, Nitro kills.
rationale.goldenRule: Inferior MI + Clear Lungs + Hypotension = RV Infarct. GIVE FLUIDS, HOLD NITRO.

steps.description: Identify Inferior MI + Hypotension + Clear Lungs.

difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Always get a V4R (Right sided ECG) on Inferior MIs before giving Nitro.

mnemonic.title: Right needs Fluid
mnemonic.content: Fill the tank (RV) to prime the pump (LV).

referenceInfo.anatomy: RCA supplies Inferior wall and RV.
referenceInfo.physiology: RV failure impairs LV filling. Increasing CVP (Preload) pushes blood through pulmonary circuit.
referenceInfo.pharm: Nitrates venodilate, dropping preload. Bad for RV infarct.

structure.prompt: Complete the intervention plan.
structure.text: The patient is experiencing a %{d1}. The nurse should immediately hold %{d2} and prepare to administer %{d3} to maintain cardiac output.

d1,.whyCorrect: ST elevation in II, III, aVF (Inferior) combined with V4R elevation, clear lungs, and hypotension is diagnostic of Right Ventricular Infarction.

distractorRationales.o2,: Anterior Wall MI presents with ST elevation in V1-V4 and typically causes pulmonary edema (crackles), unlike the clear lungs seen here.

d2,.whyCorrect: Nitroglycerin is contraindicated in RV Infarction because it reduces preload. The failing RV relies entirely on high preload to push blood to the left heart.

distractorRationales.o4,: Aspirin is essential for all STEMI patients and should not be held unless there is a severe allergy or active hemorrhage.

d3,.whyCorrect: Fluid resuscitation maximizes preload (Starling's Law), helping the weak RV generate enough pressure to fill the left ventricle.

distractorRationales.o6,: Furosemide reduces preload (diuresis), which would worsen hypotension and cardiac output in a preload-dependent RV infarct.

rationale.answerAnalysis: Right Ventricular Infarctions are preload-dependent. Vasodilators like Nitroglycerin decrease preload and can precipitate severe hypotension and shock. The priority is to maintain preload with IV fluids.
rationale.trap: Giving Nitroglycerin because it's an MI protocol. In RV MI, this is contraindicated due to hypotension risk.
rationale.goldenRule: Inferior MI + Hypotension = Rule out RV Infarct. Avoid Nitro.

distractorRationales.o2,: Administering Nitroglycerin in the presence of an RV infarct and hypotension (BP 88/54) is contraindicated as it will worsen the shock state.

rationale.coreConcept: Unstable Tachycardia management requires electricity over drugs.
rationale.caseSummary: Patient has Afib RVR and is hemodynamically unstable (Hypotension + Altered mental status + Shock signs).
rationale.answerAnalysis: According to ACLS algorithms, unstable tachycardia (hypotension, altered mental status, signs of shock) mandates immediate Synchronized Cardioversion. Medications like Diltiazem take too long and are vasodilators that may worsen the hypotension.
rationale.trap: Choosing medication (Diltiazem) first because it is less invasive. In an unstable patient, delay is dangerous.
rationale.goldenRule: Unstable Tachycardia = Electricity (Cardioversion). Stable = Drugs.

structure.prompt: Complete the rationale for the priority intervention.
structure.text: The patient is displaying signs of hemodynamic instability; therefore, the nurse should prioritize %{d1} instead of medication administration to prevent %{d2}.

d1,.whyCorrect: Synchronized cardioversion delivers a shock timed with the QRS complex to terminate the arrhythmia without causing VFib. It is the ACLS treatment for unstable tachycardia with a pulse.

distractorRationales.o2,: Defibrillation is an unsynchronized shock used for pulseless VTach or VFib. This patient has a pulse.

d2,.whyCorrect: Immediate restoration of sinus rhythm is needed to restore cardiac output and prevent complete cardiovascular collapse in this hypotensive patient.

distractorRationales.o4,: R-on-T phenomenon is a complication of *unsynchronized* shocks (defibrillation) on a live heart, not a consequence of delaying treatment per se, though avoiding it is why we sync.

rationale.coreConcept: Acute Pulmonary Edema management focuses on preload reduction and oxygenation.
rationale.caseSummary: Patient in flash pulmonary edema (pink frothy sputum, hypoxia). High BP indicates high afterload.
rationale.answerAnalysis: BiPAP (Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation) is the priority respiratory intervention. It pushes fluid out of the alveoli (PEEP) and reduces venous return (Preload), helping the heart. Increasing O2 flow alone is insufficient for alveolar flooding.
rationale.trap: Simply increasing nasal cannula flow. This does not fix the V/Q mismatch caused by fluid in the alveoli.
rationale.goldenRule: NIV (BiPAP/CPAP) is the bridge to intubation for CHF exacerbation.

Need Positive Pressure to recruit alveoli.

structure.prompt: Complete the respiratory management plan.
structure.text: The patient is exhibiting signs of acute pulmonary edema; therefore, the nurse should advocate for %{d1} to decrease preload and improve oxygenation by %{d2}.

options.text: forcing fluid out of the alveoli
increasing the fraction of inspired oxygen

d1,.whyCorrect: BiPAP provides Positive End-Expiratory Pressure (PEEP) which recruits alveoli and physically pushes fluid back into the vasculature, while also reducing venous return (preload) to the overloaded heart.

distractorRationales.o2,: High-flow nasal cannula provides oxygen but lacks the significant PEEP required to manage severe alveolar flooding and reduce cardiac workload effectively.

d2,.whyCorrect: The positive pressure mechanism of BiPAP counteracts the hydrostatic pressure in the capillaries, effectively shifting fluid out of the alveolar space to restore gas exchange.

distractorRationales.o4,: While increasing FiO2 helps, the primary mechanism benefit of BiPAP in CHF is the pressure effect on fluid mechanics and preload, not just oxygen concentration.

rationale.coreConcept: Retroperitoneal Hemorrhage is a hidden but lethal complication of femoral access.
rationale.caseSummary: Post-cath patient with hypotension, tachycardia, and back/flank pain, but a 'soft' groin site. This is classic Retroperitoneal Bleed.
rationale.answerAnalysis: Bleeding from a high femoral puncture can track backwards into the retroperitoneum. The groin site will look normal (soft/flat), but the patient will have back pain and signs of hypovolemic shock (Hypotension/Tachycardia/Hgb drop).
rationale.trap: Ruling out bleeding because the groin site looks normal. Retroperitoneal bleeds are internal and invisible externally.
rationale.goldenRule: Post-Cath Hypotension + Back Pain = Retroperitoneal Bleed until proven otherwise.

rationale.coreConcept: Cardiac Tamponade recognition involves Beck's Triad and Pulsus Paradoxus.
rationale.caseSummary: Patient has Pericarditis risk (SLE) presenting with Beck's Triad (Hypotension, JVD, Muffled sounds) + Pulsus Paradoxus.
rationale.answerAnalysis: This is classic Cardiac Tamponade. The fluid compresses the heart, preventing filling. This is an Obstructive Shock. The immediate life-saving intervention is Pericardiocentesis to drain the fluid.
rationale.trap: Confusing Tamponade with Tension Pneumothorax (both have JVD/Hypotension). However, Tamponade has muffled heart sounds; Pneumo has absent breath sounds.
rationale.goldenRule: Beck's Triad = Tamponade.

rationale.caseSummary: Patient presents with classic signs of fluid overload (CHF exacerbation): elevated BNP, crackles, edema, and orthopnea.
rationale.answerAnalysis: Furosemide is a loop diuretic that inhibits sodium reabsorption, causing diuresis. The expected outcome is increased urine output, which reduces preload and pulmonary congestion, thereby improving oxygenation.
rationale.trap: Confusing diuresis with vasodilation. While loop diuretics have a mild venodilatory effect, their primary therapeutic action in this acute phase is volume removal via the kidneys.
rationale.goldenRule: In Acute Heart Failure: Unload the volume (Diuretics) to unload the lungs (Oxygenation).

rationale.caseSummary: Patient with A-Fib has a subtherapeutic INR (1.2), increasing the risk of clot formation in the atria.
rationale.answerAnalysis: Atrial Fibrillation causes blood stasis in the atria, leading to clot formation. If a clot leaves the heart, it travels to the brain causing a stroke. Warfarin is an anticoagulant used to prevent this. A low INR indicates the blood is 'too thick' (clotting risk).
rationale.trap: Thinking the priority is rate control. While HR is 112, the immediate life-threatening risk of a subtherapeutic INR in a patient with history of stroke is a thromboembolic event.
rationale.goldenRule: A-Fib = Stasis = Clots = Stroke. Anticoagulation is non-negotiable.

rationale.caseSummary: Patient presents with stable SVT. First line is vagal maneuvers, followed by Adenosine.
rationale.answerAnalysis: Adenosine temporarily blocks the AV node to break the reentry circuit causing SVT. Because its half-life is <10 seconds, it must be pushed rapidly and flushed immediately to reach the heart before metabolizing. It causes a brief period of asystole (pause).
rationale.trap: Pushing slowly. If pushed slowly, the red blood cells metabolize the drug before it reaches the heart, rendering it ineffective.

points: Use large bore IV in AC (closest to heart).

structure.prompt: Complete the procedure for Adenosine administration.

distractorRationales.o4,: While the onset is also fast, the driving reason for the rapid push technique is the rapid elimination (half-life), not just the onset.

rationale.answerAnalysis: According to current guidelines, a systolic BP of 130-139 or diastolic 80-89 is classified as Stage 1 Hypertension. The initial management for this stage (if low risk) is lifestyle modification (diet, exercise) before medication.

rationale.coreConcept: Left vs Right Heart Failure symptoms.
rationale.caseSummary: Patient presents with pulmonary symptoms (crackles, orthopnea).
rationale.answerAnalysis: The Left Ventricle pumps to the body. Failure causes backup into the Lungs (Left = Lungs), leading to crackles, dyspnea, and orthopnea. Right ventricular failure backs up to the body (Rest of body = Right), causing edema and JVD.
rationale.trap: Confusing peripheral edema with pulmonary symptoms.
rationale.goldenRule: Left = Lungs. Right = Rest of body.

difficulty.label: Novice/Recall
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Trace the blood flow backwards from the failing ventricle.

mnemonic.title: L for Lungs
mnemonic.content: Left-sided failure causes Lung symptoms.

referenceInfo.anatomy: Pulmonary veins drain into Left Atrium.
referenceInfo.physiology: Increased LA pressure transmits to pulmonary capillaries, causing fluid leak.

structure.prompt: Complete the pathophysiology description.
structure.text: The presence of bilateral crackles and orthopnea indicates %{d1} heart failure, resulting in fluid backup into the %{d2}.

d1,.whyCorrect: Left-sided heart failure causes blood to back up from the left ventricle into the left atrium and then into the pulmonary vasculature.

distractorRationales.o2,: Right-sided heart failure causes backup into the systemic venous circulation (jugular veins, liver, extremities), not the lungs.

d2,.whyCorrect: The backup of pressure in the pulmonary vessels forces fluid into the alveoli, causing crackles (pulmonary edema).

distractorRationales.o4,: Peripheral edema is a sign of Right-sided failure or gravity dependence, not the direct result of Left-sided failure backing up.

rationale.answerAnalysis: Warfarin works by inhibiting Vitamin K dependent clotting factors. Therefore, sudden changes in Vitamin K intake (Leafy green vegetables) can alter the INR. Patients should maintain a CONSISTENT intake, not necessarily avoid it completely. INR is the lab monitored.
rationale.trap: Thinking they must eliminate all green vegetables. Consistency is the key.
rationale.goldenRule: Warfarin = INR monitoring + Consistent Vitamin K.

distractorRationales.o2,: aPTT is used to monitor Heparin therapy, not Warfarin.

d2,.whyCorrect: Vitamin K (found in leafy greens) reduces the effectiveness of Warfarin. Sudden increases can cause clots; sudden decreases can cause bleeding. Consistency is key.

rationale.answerAnalysis: Retroperitoneal hemorrhage is a life-threatening complication of femoral access. Hypotension is a late sign of significant volume loss.

rationale.caseSummary: Patient with bradycardia and hypotension showing AV dissociation.
rationale.answerAnalysis: Third-degree block is a complete dissociation between P waves (atria) and QRS complexes (ventricles). The P waves march out at their own rate, and QRS at a slower rate. This is a medical emergency requiring pacing because the escape rhythm is unreliable and slow (HR 42 + Hypotension = Unstable).
rationale.trap: Thinking this is simple sinus bradycardia or 2nd degree block. The dissociation (random PR intervals) defines 3rd degree.
rationale.goldenRule: If P's and Q's don't agree, then you have a Third Degree.

difficulty.label: Evaluation
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Identify the independence of atrial and ventricular activity.

mnemonic.title: Complete Block
mnemonic.content: Ps march, Qs march, no relationship.

referenceInfo.physiology: Ventricular escape rhythm maintains life (slow/wide).
referenceInfo.pharm: Atropine is often ineffective in 3rd degree block (infra-nodal).

structure.prompt: Highlight the telemetry findings and symptoms that indicate a Third-Degree Heart Block requiring pacing.
structure.text: Patient reports lightheadedness. Telemetry shows a ventricular rate of 42 bpm and an atrial rate of 80 bpm. The PR intervals are variable with no pattern. Blood pressure is 90/50 mmHg. The QRS complex is wide. Patient has a history of previous MI.

h1,.whyCorrect: N/A
h1,.whyIncorrect: Lightheadedness is a symptom of hypoperfusion, but not a specific ECG finding defining the type of block.

h2,.whyCorrect: Severe bradycardia (42 bpm) is the result of the slow ventricular escape rhythm characteristic of complete heart block.

h3,.whyCorrect: An atrial rate (80) faster than and independent of the ventricular rate (42) confirms AV dissociation.

h4,.whyCorrect: Variable PR intervals prove there is no relationship between atria and ventricles (AV Dissociation), diagnostic for 3rd Degree Block.

h5,.whyCorrect: Hypotension (90/50) confirms the rhythm is unstable, necessitating immediate intervention (Pacing).

h6,.whyIncorrect: A wide QRS indicates a ventricular escape rhythm but can exist in other conditions; it is not the primary diagnostic criteria for the block itself.

h7,.whyIncorrect: History is context, not an acute diagnostic finding.

rationale.caseSummary: Young patient with positional chest pain and diffuse ST elevation.
rationale.answerAnalysis: This is classic Pericarditis (Positional pain, Friction rub, Diffuse ST elevation). It mimics MI but the treatment is NSAIDs, not Cath Lab. Distinguishing the friction rub and pain pattern is key. Elevated Troponin can happen (Myopericarditis) but is usually mild.
rationale.trap: Seeing ST elevation and triggering a STEMI code. Diffuse STE (all leads) vs Regional STE (vascular territory) is the differentiator.
rationale.goldenRule: Diffuse ST Elevation + Positional Pain = Pericarditis.

Auscultation reveals a scratchy, high-pitched sound at the left sternal border. Troponin is mildly elevated (0.08). Patient has a low-grade fever. Skin is warm and dry.

h1,.whyCorrect: Positional pain (better leaning forward, worse lying flat) is the hallmark symptom of pericarditis, distinct from the constant pressure of MI.

h2,.whyCorrect: Diffuse ST elevation (in multiple non-contiguous leads) points to global pericardial inflammation rather than a specific coronary artery occlusion (regional STE).

h3,.whyCorrect: A pericardial friction rub (scratchy sound) is pathognomonic for pericarditis.

h4,.whyCorrect: N/A
h4,.whyIncorrect: Elevated troponin can occur in both MI and Pericarditis (Myopericarditis), so it does not distinguish between them.

h5,.whyIncorrect: Fever is non-specific and can be seen in both viral pericarditis and post-MI syndrome (Dressler's).

h6,.whyIncorrect: Warm skin is a normal perfusion finding, not a diagnostic differentiator.

nursesNotes.entry: Chest tube output was 200mL/hr for the last 2 hours, now suddenly 0mL in the last hour. CVP increased from 8 to 18. BP dropped to 85/50.

rationale.coreConcept: Cardiac Tamponade from Blocked Chest Tubes.
rationale.caseSummary: Post-CABG patient with sudden cessation of drainage and hemodynamic collapse.
rationale.answerAnalysis: In a post-op cardiac patient, high chest tube output followed by SUDDEN cessation suggests a clot blocking the tube, not resolution of bleeding. The blood is now trapped in the mediastinum/pericardium, causing acute tamponade (High CVP, Low BP, Tachycardia). This requires immediate surgical re-exploration or tube milking (if per protocol).
rationale.trap: Thinking the bleeding stopped because the output is 0. Look at the CVP - it went UP, meaning the fluid is trapped inside.
rationale.goldenRule: Sudden stop in drainage + Hemodynamic instability = Tamponade.

difficulty.label: Evaluation
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Correlate output with hemodynamics. 0 output is bad if the patient is crashing.

mnemonic.title: Clogged Pipe
mnemonic.content: Zero flow, Pressure low (BP), CVP grow.

referenceInfo.physiology: Trapped blood compresses heart chambers.

structure.prompt: Highlight the findings indicating acute cardiac tamponade due to chest tube obstruction.
structure.text: Chest tube output suddenly dropped to 0 mL this hour after being 200 mL/hr. CVP increased to 18 mmHg. Blood pressure dropped to 85/50 mmHg. Heart rate increased to 115 bpm. Skin is cool and mottled. Urine output is 10 mL this hour.

h1,.whyCorrect: Sudden cessation of high-volume drainage suggests tube occlusion (clot), trapping blood in the pericardium.

h2,.whyCorrect: A rising CVP (18 mmHg) indicates increased pressure around the heart (obstructive shock), confirming the trapped blood theory.

h3,.whyCorrect: Hypotension is the direct result of the tamponade physiology (reduced filling = reduced output).

h4,.whyCorrect: N/A
h4,.whyIncorrect: Tachycardia is a compensatory mechanism for shock, but less specific to the *cause* (tamponade) than the combination of 0 output + High CVP.

h5,.whyIncorrect: Cool skin is a general sign of shock, not specific to the mechanism of blocked tubes.

h6,.whyIncorrect: Low urine output is a downstream effect of hypotension, confirming shock but not the etiology.

rationale.caseSummary: Patient with known severe AS faints during exertion.
rationale.answerAnalysis: In Aortic Stenosis, the outflow tract is narrowed (fixed obstruction). During exertion, the body demands more oxygen (vasodilation occurs in muscles). However, the heart CANNOT increase Cardiac Output past the obstruction. This mismatch (Vasodilation + Fixed CO) causes global cerebral hypoperfusion = Syncope. Nitroglycerin is dangerous because it drops preload, which the stiff heart relies on.
rationale.trap: Thinking Nitroglycerin is good for all chest pain/cardiac issues. In AS, Nitro can cause fatal hypotension.
rationale.goldenRule: Fixed Cardiac Output means NO exertion and CAUTION with nitrates.

difficulty.label: Analysis
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Recognize that 'Exertional Syncope' in an elderly patient is AS until proven otherwise.

mnemonic.title: SAD
mnemonic.content: Syncope, Angina, Dyspnea.

referenceInfo.anatomy: Aortic valve sits between LV and Aorta.
referenceInfo.physiology: Stenosis increases LV pressure load (afterload).

structure.prompt: Complete the analysis of the client's condition.
structure.text: The client's syncope is caused by the heart's inability to increase %{d1} during physical exertion. The nurse should instruct the client to %{d2}.

d1,.whyCorrect: Aortic stenosis creates a fixed obstruction. When the body demands more blood (exertion), the heart physically cannot pump more blood (Cardiac Output) through the narrow valve, leading to a drop in brain perfusion.

distractorRationales.o2,: The heart rate CAN and does increase during exertion (compensatory tachycardia), but it is ineffective at maintaining pressure because of the mechanical blockage.

d2,.whyCorrect: Until the valve is replaced, the only safety measure is limiting demand. Strenuous activity risks sudden cardiac death.

distractorRationales.o4,: Nitroglycerin reduces preload. A heart with aortic stenosis is preload-dependent (needs volume to push through the valve). Giving Nitro can cause severe hypotension and syncope.

rationale.caseSummary: Child presents with classic CRASH and Burn signs: Conjunctivitis, Rash, Adenopathy, Strawberry tongue, Hand/foot swelling, and Fever > 5 days.
rationale.answerAnalysis: Kawasaki Disease is a systemic vasculitis. The major complication is Coronary Artery Aneurysms (dilation of heart vessels). The priority treatment is IVIG (to reduce immune response) and Aspirin (anti-inflammatory/anti-platelet). This is the ONE pediatric exception where Aspirin is given despite Reye's syndrome risk.
rationale.trap: Withholding Aspirin because 'Kids shouldn't have Aspirin'. In Kawasaki, the benefit (heart protection) outweighs the Reye's risk.
rationale.goldenRule: Fever > 5 days + Strawberry Tongue = Kawasaki.

difficulty.label: Analysis
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Recognize the 'Strawberry Tongue' as the key discriminator.

mnemonic.title: CRASH and Burn

structure.prompt: Complete the diagnostic analysis.
structure.text: The child's clinical presentation is consistent with %{d1}. The priority goal of treatment is to prevent the development of %{d2}.

d1,.whyCorrect: Prolonged fever (>5 days) combined with 'strawberry tongue', conjunctivitis, and extremity changes is the classic presentation of Kawasaki Disease.

distractorRationales.o2,: Scarlet fever also presents with strawberry tongue but typically includes a 'sandpaper' rash and responds to antibiotics; it does not usually cause the prolonged fever and extremity edema seen here.

d2,.whyCorrect: The most serious complication of Kawasaki disease is inflammation of the coronary arteries, leading to aneurysms and potential myocardial infarction.

distractorRationales.o4,: Rheumatic heart disease is a complication of untreated Strep throat (Scarlet Fever), damaging the valves, not the coronary arteries.

nursesNotes.entry: ECG strip shows regular P waves at 80 bpm and regular QRS complexes at 38 bpm. There is no relationship between P waves and QRS complexes.

rationale.caseSummary: Patient presents with severe bradycardia and AV dissociation.
rationale.answerAnalysis: When P waves and QRS complexes march out independently (AV Dissociation), it is a 3rd Degree Block. No impulses pass from atria to ventricles. The ventricles are beating on their own slow escape rhythm (38 bpm). This is a LETHAL rhythm because the escape pacemaker can fail. Treatment is PACING (Transcutaneous first, then Transvenous). Atropine is often ineffective because the block is usually below the AV node.
rationale.trap: Trying Atropine repeatedly while the patient deteriorates. In 3rd degree block, move quickly to Pacing.
rationale.goldenRule: P's and Q's don't agree = 3rd Degree. Get the Pacer.

difficulty.label: Analysis
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Assess stability. Symptomatic 3rd degree block requires electricity (pacing).

mnemonic.title: Divorced Heart
mnemonic.content: Atria (P) and Ventricles (QRS) are divorced and living separate lives.

cheatSheet.title: Heart Block Poems
points: 2nd T1: Husband stays later, then misses dinner (Drop)
2nd T2: Husband comes home sometimes (Random Drop)

referenceInfo.physiology: Total blockage of electrical conduction.
referenceInfo.pharm: Dopamine/Epinephrine drips can support BP/HR if pacer delayed.

structure.prompt: Complete the interpretation and plan.
structure.text: The ECG finding of AV dissociation confirms %{d1}. Due to the client's hypotension, the nurse should immediately prepare for %{d2}.

d1,.whyCorrect: Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes (they march out independently) is the hallmark of Third-Degree (Complete) Heart Block.

distractorRationales.o2,: Wenckebach is characterized by progressive lengthening of the PR interval until a beat is dropped, not total dissociation.

d2,.whyCorrect: With a heart rate of 38 and hypotension (symptomatic bradycardia), the priority is increasing the heart rate to improve cardiac output. Pacing is the definitive treatment for 3rd-degree block.

distractorRationales.o4,: Cardioversion is used for tachyarrhythmias (fast rhythms), not bradycardia. Shocking a slow heart could cause asystole.

rationale.caseSummary: Patient presents with the triad of AAA rupture: 1) Hypotension, 2) Flank/Back pain, 3) Pulsatile mass.
rationale.answerAnalysis: Sudden severe back pain combined with hypotension (Shock) in an older smoker is a ruptured AAA until proven otherwise. This is a surgical emergency. The nurse must establish large-bore IV access immediately for massive transfusion/resuscitation. Pain meds are secondary to saving their life.
rationale.trap: Thinking it is Kidney Stones (Renal Colic). Kidney stones cause pain but rarely shock (hypotension).
rationale.goldenRule: Back Pain + Hypotension = Ruptured AAA.

difficulty.label: Analysis
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Do not palpate the mass vigorously! Get IVs and get to OR.

mnemonic.title: AAA Triad
mnemonic.content: Abdominal pain, Hypotension, Pulsatile mass.

referenceInfo.physiology: Rupture causes massive retroperitoneal hemorrhage (Hypovolemic shock).

structure.prompt: Complete the assessment analysis.
structure.text: The combination of hypotension, pulsatile mass, and sudden back pain indicates a likely %{d1}. The nurse should immediately %{d2}.

d1,.whyCorrect: The triad of hypotension (shock), pulsatile abdominal mass, and severe back/flank pain is the classic presentation of a ruptured AAA, a catastrophic vascular emergency.

distractorRationales.o2,: Renal calculi (kidney stones) cause severe pain but do not present with a pulsatile mass or profound hemorrhagic shock (hypotension).

d2,.whyCorrect: The patient is actively bleeding internally. Immediate large-bore IV access (14g or 16g) is critical for administering fluids and blood products to maintain perfusion until surgery.

distractorRationales.o4,: An enema increases intra-abdominal pressure and could worsen the rupture; it is contraindicated in acute abdominal emergencies.

rationale.caseSummary: Patient on Digoxin + Lasix has diarrhea (K+ loss) and now presents with toxicity signs.
rationale.answerAnalysis: Early signs of Digoxin toxicity are vague: Anorexia, Nausea, Vomiting. Late signs are visual changes (Yellow/Green halos) and arrhythmias. The most common precipitating factor is HYPOKALEMIA (low potassium), which sensitizes the heart to Digoxin. Diuretics (Lasix) and Diarrhea both cause K+ loss.
rationale.trap: Thinking it's just the 'stomach flu' continuing. The visual changes (halos) and bradycardia are the 'tell' for toxicity.
rationale.goldenRule: Low K+ = High Dig toxicity risk.

difficulty.label: Analysis
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Check Potassium first in any patient with Dig toxicity signs.

mnemonic.title: Visual Van Gogh
mnemonic.content: Van Gogh painted 'Starry Night' with yellow halos (possibly due to Digoxin toxicity).

referenceInfo.physiology: Digoxin competes with Potassium for binding sites. Less K+ = More Digoxin binds = Toxicity.

structure.prompt: Complete the clinical analysis.
structure.text: The client is exhibiting signs of %{d1}, likely precipitated by %{d2} from recent fluid losses.

d1,.whyCorrect: Anorexia, nausea, and visual disturbances (green/yellow halos) combined with bradycardia are classic signs of Digoxin toxicity.

distractorRationales.o2,: Hypertensive crisis involves severe high blood pressure and headache, not the GI and visual symptoms seen here.

d2,.whyCorrect: Hypokalemia (low potassium) potentiates the effects of Digoxin, making toxicity more likely even at normal doses. The patient's diarrhea and Lasix use likely caused the low K+.

distractorRationales.o4,: While calcium levels matter, hypokalemia is the primary electrolyte disturbance associated with diuretic use and Digoxin toxicity risk.

rationale.caseSummary: IV drug user presenting with fever and embolic signs.
rationale.answerAnalysis: Infective Endocarditis involves bacterial growth on heart valves (vegetations). These can break off (embolize). Key signs: New Murmur (vegetation on valve), Splinter Hemorrhages (micro-emboli to nail beds), Fever (infection), and Osler's Nodes/Janeway Lesions.
rationale.trap: Confusing Splinter Hemorrhages with trauma. In the context of fever + murmur, it is pathognomonic for endocarditis.
rationale.goldenRule: Fever + Murmur + IVDU = Endocarditis until proven otherwise.

difficulty.label: Evaluation
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Link the peripheral finding (nails) to the central problem (heart).

mnemonic.title: FROM JANE
mnemonic.content: Fever, Roth spots, Osler nodes, Murmur, Janeway lesions, Anemia, Nail-bed hemorrhage, Emboli.

referenceInfo.anatomy: Tricuspid valve often affected in IVDU.
referenceInfo.physiology: Bacteremia seeds the valves.

structure.text: Patient reports night sweats and fatigue. Assessment reveals a new systolic murmur at the left sternal border. There are dark splinter hemorrhages under the fingernails. Patient has a history of IV drug use. Temperature is 101.5°F. Lungs are clear to auscultation.

h1,.whyCorrect: Night sweats are a constitutional symptom of systemic infection.

h2,.whyCorrect: A new murmur indicates vegetation growth on the heart valves, disrupting blood flow.

h3,.whyCorrect: Splinter hemorrhages are caused by micro-emboli from the valve vegetations traveling to the capillaries in the nail beds.

h4,.whyCorrect: N/A
h4,.whyIncorrect: IV drug use is a risk factor (history), not an active physical assessment finding of the disease process itself.

h5,.whyCorrect: Fever confirms the infectious nature of the condition.

h6,.whyIncorrect: Clear lungs are a normal finding and do not confirm endocarditis (unless septic emboli cause pulmonary issues, which isn't present here).

rationale.answerAnalysis: The triad for AAA rupture/leak is: 1. Abdominal/Back pain (often described as tearing or gnawing), 2. Pulsatile Abdominal Mass, 3. Hypotension. The bruit indicates turbulent flow. This is a surgical emergency.
rationale.trap: Mistaking the back pain for musculoskeletal strain or kidney stones. The key differentiator is the pulsatile mass and hypotension.
rationale.goldenRule: Pulsatile Mass + Back Pain = AAA.

h3,.whyCorrect: A bruit indicates turbulent blood flow through a dilated or stenotic vessel, supporting vascular pathology.

h4,.whyCorrect: Hypotension (95/55) suggests possible rupture or leaking with internal bleeding.

h5,.whyIncorrect: Smoking is a risk factor (history), not an acute sign of the rupture itself.

h6,.whyIncorrect: Clear urine helps rule out renal colic (stones) but is not a sign of AAA.

rationale.caseSummary: Patient on Lasix (causing low K) and Digoxin presents with toxicity signs.
rationale.answerAnalysis: Hypokalemia (K < 3.5) potentiates Digoxin toxicity. The classic signs are GI symptoms (Nausea/Vomiting/Anorexia) followed by Neurological symptoms (Visual halos, confusion) and Cardiac arrhythmias (Bradycardia).
rationale.trap: Attributing nausea to a stomach bug. The visual halos and bradycardia make it specific to Digoxin.
rationale.goldenRule: Low K+ = High Dig toxicity risk.

difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Identify the electrolyte imbalance that triggered the toxicity.

structure.prompt: Highlight the findings indicating probable Digoxin toxicity.
structure.text: Patient reports nausea and vomiting for 2 days. She describes seeing yellow halos around lights. Heart rate is 52 bpm. Potassium level is 3.1 mEq/L. Patient takes Furosemide daily. Lungs have crackles at bases. There is 1+ pitting edema in ankles.

h1,.whyCorrect: GI symptoms like nausea and vomiting are often the earliest signs of Digoxin toxicity.

h2,.whyCorrect: Visual disturbances (yellow/green halos or blurred vision) are a hallmark neurological sign of toxicity.

h3,.whyCorrect: Bradycardia (52 bpm) results from the vagomimetic effect of toxic Digoxin levels.

h4,.whyCorrect: Hypokalemia (3.1) predisposes the patient to toxicity because potassium and digoxin compete for binding sites on the heart.

h5,.whyIncorrect: Furosemide is the cause of the hypokalemia (medication history), not a sign of the toxicity itself.

h6,.whyIncorrect: Crackles are a sign of the underlying Heart Failure, not toxicity.

h7,.whyIncorrect: Edema is a sign of Heart Failure, not toxicity.

rationale.caseSummary: Afib patient off anticoagulants presents with acute limb ischemia.
rationale.answerAnalysis: Acute Arterial Occlusion is a surgical emergency characterized by the 6 Ps: Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Paresthesia, Paralysis, Poikilothermia (Coldness). This distinguishes it from Venous issues (Warm, Edematous) or Chronic PAD (Hair loss, Claudication).
rationale.trap: Thinking this is DVT. DVT legs are Red, Swollen, and Warm. Arterial legs are Pale, Thin, and Cold.
rationale.goldenRule: Pain + Pallor + Pulselessness = Ischemia.

difficulty.label: Evaluation
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Memorize the 6 Ps. Cold/Pale is always Arterial.

mnemonic.title: 6 P's
mnemonic.content: Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Paresthesia, Paralysis, Poikilothermia.

structure.prompt: Highlight the findings indicating Acute Arterial Occlusion.
structure.text: Right leg is pale and cool to touch. Patient reports severe pain and numbness in the foot. The right pedal pulse is absent by Doppler. Capillary refill is delayed (>3 seconds). The left leg is warm with a palpable pulse. Patient has chronic atrial fibrillation.

h1,.whyCorrect: Pallor (pale) and Poikilothermia (cool) are classic signs of arterial blood flow blockage.

h2,.whyCorrect: Severe pain distal to the occlusion is the first sign of ischemia.

h3,.whyCorrect: Paresthesia (numbness) indicates nerve ischemia, a sign of advanced limb threat.

h4,.whyCorrect: Pulselessness confirms complete or near-complete arterial obstruction.

h5,.whyCorrect: Delayed capillary refill indicates poor tissue perfusion.

h6,.whyIncorrect: Findings in the unaffected leg (warm/palpable) are normal and used for comparison, not the problem.

h7,.whyIncorrect: Atrial fibrillation is the cause (history), not an assessment finding of the limb itself.

rationale.caseSummary: Dialysis patient with missed session presents with dangerously high Potassium (7.2).
rationale.answerAnalysis: Hyperkalemia causes predictable EKG progression: 1. Peaked T waves (Earliest), 2. QRS Widening, 3. Loss of P waves, 4. Sine Wave -> Asystole. Muscle weakness and palpitations are clinical symptoms. This is an emergency requiring cardiac stabilization (Calcium Gluconate) and K+ shifting (Insulin/D50).
rationale.trap: Ignoring the T waves because the patient is 'stable'. 7.2 is lethal potential.
rationale.goldenRule: Peaked T's = High K.

structure.prompt: Highlight the findings indicating severe hyperkalemia.
structure.text: EKG shows tall, peaked T-waves and a widened QRS complex. Patient reports muscle weakness and palpitations. Potassium level is 7.2 mEq/L. Patient has a history of End Stage Renal Disease. Blood pressure is 130/80 mmHg.

h1,.whyCorrect: Tall, peaked T-waves are the earliest and most specific EKG sign of hyperkalemia.

h2,.whyCorrect: Widened QRS indicates severe conduction delay from high potassium, warning of imminent cardiac arrest.

h3,.whyCorrect: Muscle weakness (ascending paralysis) occurs as high potassium affects neuromuscular transmission.

h4,.whyCorrect: Palpitations suggest cardiac irritability/arrhythmia associated with the electrolyte imbalance.

h5,.whyCorrect: Potassium of 7.2 is a critical lab value confirming the diagnosis.

h6,.whyIncorrect: ESRD is the cause (history), not a sign of the acute hyperkalemia itself.

h7,.whyIncorrect: Normal blood pressure does not rule out hyperkalemia and is not a specific sign of it.

nursesNotes.entry: Jugular Vein Distension (JVD) noted at 45 degrees. 3+ pitting edema to knees. Lungs have diffuse expiratory wheezes but are clear of crackles. Hepatomegaly palpable.

rationale.caseSummary: Patient with chronic lung disease presents with Right Heart Failure symptoms (JVD, Edema, Hepatomegaly) without Left Heart symptoms (Crackles).
rationale.answerAnalysis: This is Cor Pulmonale. Chronic lung disease (COPD) causes pulmonary hypertension (high pressure in lung arteries). The Right Ventricle struggles to pump against this high pressure, eventually failing. Signs are 'backup' into the body: JVD, Edema, Liver congestion. Lungs remain relatively clear of fluid (no crackles) because the failure is *before* the lungs.
rationale.trap: Thinking this is Left Heart Failure because of the BNP. Left HF causes Pulmonary Edema (Crackles). Right HF (Cor Pulmonale) causes Peripheral Edema.
rationale.goldenRule: COPD + Edema + JVD = Cor Pulmonale.

difficulty.label: Analysis
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Notice the absence of crackles. If lungs are clear but legs are wet, it's Right Sided.

mnemonic.title: Cor-P
mnemonic.content: COPD causes Cor Pulmonale (Right HF).

cheatSheet.title: Right vs Left HF
points: Right: Rest of Body (Edema, JVD, Liver)
Cor Pulmonale: Right HF caused by Lung Disease

referenceInfo.anatomy: Pulmonary arteries connect RV to Lungs.
referenceInfo.physiology: Hypoxia causes pulmonary vasoconstriction, raising PA pressure.

structure.prompt: Complete the diagnostic analysis.
structure.text: The client is exhibiting signs of %{d1}, primarily caused by %{d2}. The nurse expects to assess %{d3} on physical exam.

d1,.whyCorrect: The combination of severe COPD, JVD, peripheral edema, and hepatomegaly indicates failure of the right ventricle, known as Cor Pulmonale.

distractorRationales.o2,: Left-sided heart failure typically presents with pulmonary congestion (crackles, orthopnea), which is absent in this patient's lung exam.

d2,.whyCorrect: Chronic lung disease (COPD) leads to chronic hypoxia, causing constriction of pulmonary vessels (Pulmonary Hypertension). This high afterload causes the Right Ventricle to fail.

distractorRationales.o4,: Systemic hypertension causes Left Ventricular hypertrophy and failure, not isolated Right Ventricular failure.

d3,.whyCorrect: In isolated Right Heart Failure, fluid backs up into the venous system (body), not the lungs. Therefore, lung sounds often lack the fluid crackles seen in Left HF (though wheezes from COPD may be present).

distractorRationales.o6,: Crackles indicate fluid inside the alveoli, a hallmark of Left-Sided failure backing up into the pulmonary vasculature.

history.note: Jugular Vein Distension (JVD) noted at 45 degrees. 3+ pitting edema to knees. Lungs have diffuse expiratory wheezes but are clear of crackles. Hepatomegaly palpable.

Day 4 post-Inferior MI. Doing well until 30 minutes ago, suddenly developed flash pulmonary edema and hypotension.

nursesNotes.entry: New loud holosystolic murmur auscultated at apex. Skin cool and clammy. Massive pink frothy sputum.

rationale.caseSummary: Post-MI patient develops sudden cardiogenic shock and pulmonary edema with a new murmur.
rationale.answerAnalysis: Papillary muscle rupture is a catastrophic complication of MI (usually days 3-5). The muscle holding the Mitral Valve chordae snaps. The valve leaflets flail, causing massive Acute Mitral Regurgitation. Blood blasts back into the LA -> Lungs -> Flash Edema. The heart can't pump forward -> Shock. Requires immediate surgery.
rationale.trap: Thinking this is just recurrent MI. The *New Murmur* is the critical cue distinguishing structural failure from ischemic failure.
rationale.goldenRule: Post-MI + New Murmur + Shock = Valve/Muscle Rupture.

difficulty.label: Analysis
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Focus on the timing (days post-MI) and the murmur location (Apex).

mnemonic.title: MR. PASS
mnemonic.content: Mitral Regurgitation - Papillary muscle rupture, Acute, Sudden Shock.

cheatSheet.title: MI Complications
points: VSD: Holosystolic murmur at sternal border
Papillary Rupture: Holosystolic murmur at Apex

referenceInfo.anatomy: Papillary muscles attach Mitral valve to LV wall.
referenceInfo.physiology: Rupture causes wide open valve during systole.
referenceInfo.pharm: Nitroprusside (if BP allows) to reduce afterload; IABP for stabilization.

structure.prompt: Complete the interpretation of the client's deterioration.
structure.text: The development of a new holosystolic murmur at the apex combined with acute pulmonary edema suggests %{d1}. This complication results in massive %{d2}, requiring emergent surgical intervention.

d1,.whyCorrect: Rupture of the papillary muscle (often 3-5 days post-MI) causes the mitral valve leaflets to flail, creating a new loud murmur at the apex and sudden hemodynamic collapse.

distractorRationales.o2,: Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD) also causes a holosystolic murmur but typically at the left sternal border, not the apex, and is associated with a 'thrill'.

d2,.whyCorrect: The flail mitral leaflet allows blood to regurgitate forcefully into the left atrium during systole, causing an immediate rise in pulmonary pressures (Flash Edema) and loss of forward flow (Shock).

distractorRationales.o4,: Aortic stenosis is a chronic narrowing, not an acute regurgitant event associated with MI rupture.

history.note: New loud holosystolic murmur auscultated at apex. Skin cool and clammy. Massive pink frothy sputum.

Admitted for Methadone overdose monitoring. Complained of palpitations.

nursesNotes.entry: Telemetry alarm sounding. ECG shows QRS complexes twisting around the isoelectric line. Rate 200+.

rationale.caseSummary: Patient with QT-prolonging drug (Methadone) and electrolytes imbalances develops polymorphic VT.
rationale.answerAnalysis: The ECG description ('twisting of points') is classic Torsades de Pointes. This is a lethal arrhythmia caused by a Prolonged QT interval. Common causes are Drugs (Antiarrhythmics, Methadone, Antibiotics) and Low Electrolytes (Magnesium/Potassium). The specific antidote/treatment is IV Magnesium Sulfate (even if Mg is normal, but here it is low).
rationale.trap: Thinking this is regular V-Tach and giving Amiodarone. Amiodarone PROLONGS the QT further and can kill a patient with Torsades. You must recognize the 'twisting'.
rationale.goldenRule: Twisting points = Torsades = Give Magnesium.

difficulty.label: Analysis
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Check the QT interval on the previous strip. If long (>500ms), the new rhythm is Torsades.

mnemonic.title: Mg for TdP
mnemonic.content: Magnesium for Torsades de Pointes.

referenceInfo.physiology: Delayed repolarization (Long QT) allows 'R on T' phenomenon.

structure.prompt: Complete the rhythm analysis and plan.
structure.text: The ECG pattern is consistent with %{d1}, which is often precipitated by a %{d2}. The priority medication for this arrhythmia is %{d3}.

d1,.whyCorrect: The description of QRS complexes 'twisting around the isoelectric line' is the visual definition of Torsades de Pointes (Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia).

distractorRationales.o2,: Atrial fibrillation is irregular but narrow-complex (usually), without the shifting/twisting amplitude of Torsades.

d2,.whyCorrect: Torsades is triggered by delayed repolarization, seen on the ECG as a prolonged QT interval. Methadone and hypomagnesemia are key causes.

distractorRationales.o4,: Shortened PR intervals are associated with Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome, not Torsades.

d3,.whyCorrect: Magnesium Sulfate is the first-line treatment for Torsades de Pointes because it stabilizes the cardiac membrane and shortens the QT interval.

distractorRationales.o6,: Amiodarone is a QT-prolonging drug. Giving it to a patient with Torsades (caused by Long QT) can worsen the arrhythmia and is contraindicated.

history.note: Telemetry alarm sounding. ECG shows QRS complexes twisting around the isoelectric line. Rate 200+.

Collpased while sprinting. Woke up after 30 seconds.

nursesNotes.entry: Systolic murmur heard at left sternal border. Murmur becomes LOUDER when patient bears down (Valsalva) and SOFTER when squatting.

rationale.caseSummary: Young athlete with exertional syncope and a dynamic murmur.
rationale.answerAnalysis: HOCM is the leading cause of sudden death in young athletes. The septum is thickened, obstructing outflow. The obstruction worsens when the heart is 'empty' (decreased preload), such as during Valsalva or standing. It improves when the heart is 'full' (increased preload/afterload), such as Squatting. This is the OPPOSITE of most murmurs (like Aortic Stenosis, which gets softer with Valsalva). Prevention of Sudden Cardiac Death involves avoiding dehydration and strenuous sports.
rationale.trap: Confusing HOCM murmur with Aortic Stenosis. AS gets softer with Valsalva (less blood to flow). HOCM gets louder (more obstruction).
rationale.goldenRule: Valsalva makes HOCM Louder.

difficulty.label: Analysis
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Differentiate murmurs by maneuvers. Squatting fills the heart (softer HOCM). Valsalva empties it (louder HOCM).

mnemonic.title: Loud Squeezes
mnemonic.content: Squeezing (bearing down) makes the HOCM murmur Loud.

referenceInfo.anatomy: Hypertrophied septum blocks LV outflow tract.
referenceInfo.physiology: Obstruction is dynamic based on LV volume.
referenceInfo.pharm: Beta blockers help by slowing HR and allowing filling.

structure.prompt: Complete the risk analysis.
structure.text: The systolic murmur that increases in intensity with the Valsalva maneuver is characteristic of %{d1}. To prevent sudden cardiac death, the client must avoid %{d2}.

d1,.whyCorrect: HOCM is unique because the obstruction worsens when the ventricle volume decreases (Valsalva decreases preload). This makes the murmur LOUDER. Most other murmurs get softer with less blood flow.

distractorRationales.o2,: Aortic Stenosis gets SOFTER with Valsalva because there is less blood flowing across the stenotic valve to create noise.

d2,.whyCorrect: Dehydration reduces preload, worsening the obstruction. Strenuous exertion increases the risk of fatal arrhythmias (Sudden Cardiac Death).

distractorRationales.o4,: While a generally healthy diet is good, sodium restriction is not the primary prevention for sudden death in HOCM; volume depletion is the actual danger.

history.note: Systolic murmur heard at left sternal border. Murmur becomes LOUDER when patient bears down (Valsalva) and SOFTER when squatting.

Started on Heparin drip 5 days ago for DVT. Now reporting new pain in opposite leg.

nursesNotes.entry: Platelet count dropped from 160k to 75k overnight. New coolness noted in left toes.

rationale.caseSummary: Patient on Heparin develops a >50% drop in platelets and new clots (cool toes).
rationale.answerAnalysis: HIT is an immune reaction where antibodies activate platelets, causing them to clump (clotting) and get used up (low count). The danger is THROMBOSIS (clots), not bleeding initially. A drop in platelets >50% from baseline is the trigger. Treatment: STOP all Heparin immediately. Start a non-heparin anticoagulant (Argatroban). Do NOT give Platelets (adds fuel to the fire).
rationale.trap: Thinking low platelets = Bleeding risk only. In HIT, low platelets = Clotting risk (Paradoxical).
rationale.goldenRule: Platelets down 50%? Stop Heparin. Don't give Platelets.

difficulty.label: Analysis
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Calculate the percentage drop, not just the absolute number.

mnemonic.title: HIT the Stop Button
mnemonic.content: Stop Heparin immediately.

referenceInfo.physiology: Antibodies bind to PF4-Heparin complex, activating platelets.
referenceInfo.pharm: Argatroban is a direct thrombin inhibitor used as alternative.

structure.prompt: Complete the safety intervention.
structure.text: The 50% decrease in platelet count indicates the development of %{d1}. The nurse must immediately %{d2} and initiate a different anticoagulant, such as %{d3}.

d1,.whyCorrect: A drop in platelet count of >50% from baseline within 5-10 days of starting Heparin is diagnostic for HIT.

distractorRationales.o2,: ITP is an autoimmune condition not related to Heparin administration and typically presents with petechiae/bleeding, not new thrombosis.

d2,.whyCorrect: The immune reaction is driven by the presence of Heparin. Stopping the exposure is the only way to halt the process.

distractorRationales.o4,: Transfusing platelets adds more 'fuel to the fire', causing more clotting and worsening the thrombosis risk. It is contraindicated.

d3,.whyCorrect: The patient still requires anticoagulation for the original DVT and the new HIT clots. Argatroban is a Direct Thrombin Inhibitor safe for HIT.

distractorRationales.o6,: Warfarin is contraindicated in acute HIT because it depletes Protein C (natural anticoagulant) and can cause 'venous limb gangrene' when platelets are low.

history.note: Platelet count dropped from 160k to 75k overnight. New coolness noted in left toes.

Ran out of BP meds 3 days ago. Vision is blurry.

nursesNotes.entry: Patient is anxious. Reports seeing double.

rationale.caseSummary: Patient with extremely high BP and signs of target organ damage.
rationale.answerAnalysis: Hypertensive Emergency is defined by elevated BP (>180/120) WITH evidence of acute target organ damage (Brain, Heart, Kidneys, Eyes). Key cues here are the severity of BP, Headache/Visual changes (Brain/Eyes), and elevated Creatinine (Kidneys). Urgency has high numbers but NO organ damage.
rationale.trap: Thinking this is just Urgency because the patient is alert. The visual changes and creatinine bump define it as Emergency requiring IV meds.
rationale.goldenRule: Organ Damage = Emergency = IV Meds.

difficulty.label: Evaluation
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Find the organ damage to classify the crisis.

mnemonic.title: Change in Vision
mnemonic.content: Blurred vision + High BP = Hypertensive Encephalopathy risk.

referenceInfo.physiology: Pressure exceeds vessel capacity, causing leakage/damage.
referenceInfo.pharm: Reduce BP by max 25% in first hour to prevent ischemia.

structure.prompt: Highlight the findings that differentiate Hypertensive Emergency from Hypertensive Urgency.
structure.text: Patient presents with a blood pressure of 230/125 mmHg. He reports a severe, throbbing headache and blurred vision. He admits to missing his medications for 3 days. Lab work reveals a Creatinine of 1.8 mg/dL. Patient is alert and oriented. Heart rate is 92 bpm.

h1,.whyCorrect: Severe elevation >180/120 is the entry criterion for crisis.

h2,.whyCorrect: Headache indicates increased intracranial pressure/encephalopathy (Target Organ Damage).

h3,.whyCorrect: Visual disturbances indicate hypertensive retinopathy (Target Organ Damage).

h4,.whyCorrect: N/A
h4,.whyIncorrect: Non-compliance explains the cause but doesn't define the severity classification (Emergency vs Urgency).

h5,.whyCorrect: Elevated Creatinine indicates acute kidney injury (Target Organ Damage).

h6,.whyIncorrect: Being alert is a positive sign but does not rule out organ damage in kidneys/eyes.

h7,.whyIncorrect: HR 92 is non-specific.

history.note: Patient is anxious. Reports seeing double.

nursesNotes.entry: Patient is diaphoretic. Pain is 6/10 substernal pressure.

rationale.caseSummary: Patient with known angina presents with change in pattern (pain at rest/unrelieved).
rationale.answerAnalysis: Unstable Angina is characterized by ischemia without cell death (Negative Troponin) but with high risk features: Pain at rest, Pain unrelieved by Nitro, or New/Worsening pattern. This differentiates it from Stable Angina (exertional, relieved by rest) and NSTEMI (positive troponin).
rationale.trap: Thinking it's 'Stable' because the Troponin is negative. The clinical presentation (Pain at rest) makes it Unstable.
rationale.goldenRule: Rest pain = Unstable.

difficulty.label: Evaluation
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Identify the 'red flags' that move this from Stable to Unstable.

mnemonic.title: Unstable Features
mnemonic.content: Rest pain, Refractory (no relief), Recent acceleration.

referenceInfo.physiology: Supply/demand mismatch at rest.

structure.prompt: Highlight the findings indicating Unstable Angina rather than Stable Angina.
structure.text: Patient reports chest pain that woke him from sleep. The pain was not relieved by 3 nitroglycerin tablets. Patient has a history of stable angina. Skin is diaphoretic. EKG shows ST-segment depression. Troponin I is negative (<0.01).

h1,.whyCorrect: Pain occurring at rest (sleep) is a definitive sign of Unstable Angina.

h2,.whyCorrect: Pain refractory to nitroglycerin indicates worsening ischemia and instability.

h3,.whyCorrect: N/A
h3,.whyIncorrect: History provides context, but the current symptoms define the new classification.

h4,.whyCorrect: Diaphoresis is a sign of sympathetic discharge due to acute ischemia.

h6,.whyIncorrect: A negative troponin is consistent with Unstable Angina, but does not indicate the *instability* itself (it just rules out infarction for now).
